title: Aching hands, knees, hips and back in a 56-year-old farmer
desc: This station involves a focused joint pain history and musculoskeletal examination of a 56-year-old farmer in general practice. She has 6 months of gradually worsening mechanical pain in her hands, knees, hips and lower back. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her inflammatory markers, serology, kidney function and hand X-ray, then outlines non-surgical management of osteoarthritis led by exercise and weight loss, and safety-nets.
focus: Polyarticular joint pain: telling osteoarthritis from inflammatory arthritis in the history, examination and results, then evidence-based management of osteoarthritis in general practice
stem: You are a final-year medical student on a General Practice placement in a regional town about an hour from the city. Laila Thomas, a 56-year-old farmer, has made an appointment because of pain in her joints.
tasks: Take a focused history from Ms Thomas and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you her blood results and the report of her hand X-rays. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Laila Thomas, a 56-year-old farmer. You are friendly and a bit matter-of-fact about the pain. You are right-handed. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "My joints have been aching for months now and it's slowly getting worse."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Onset and course: it came on gradually over about 6 months and has slowly got worse.
  • Site: both sides of your lower back, both hips, both knees and both hands. If asked where in the hands, point to the end finger joints, the middle finger joints and the base of each thumb. It does not travel down your legs.
  • Character: "A deep ache."
  • Severity: 5 out of 10 at its worst.
  • Worse: moving, especially walking and standing (weight-bearing), and gripping things.
  • Better: resting.
  • Anything that set it off: "I can't think of anything specific."
  • Stiffness: "I'm very stiff in the morning, but it's gone by the time I've had my first cup of tea" (under 30 minutes). Brief stiffness again after sitting for a while.
  • Clicking: "My joints do click a bit," especially the knees.
  • Movement: you can't bend your knees, hips or back as far as you used to.
  • Lumps: over the last year or two the finger joints have become "a bit knobbly". They are hard, not puffy or soft.
  • Impact: "It's making it really hard for me to do the 15-minute walk around the farm, and I can't even open jars now!"

Other symptoms (give only when asked; the answer to all of these is no):

  • No soft, puffy, hot or red joints. No stiffness lasting hours. No lumps on the elbows. No unusual tiredness.
  • No sudden, very painful swollen joint, ever. No previous gout.
  • No aching or stiffness across the shoulders or upper arms. No headaches, tenderness of the scalp, jaw pain on chewing or change in vision.
  • No rashes, sun sensitivity, mouth ulcers, hair loss, or fingers changing colour in the cold.
  • No psoriasis or nail changes. No diarrhoea, blood in the stool or bowel problems. No recent infections, urinary or genital symptoms, or red, sore eyes.
  • No fevers, night sweats or weight loss (your weight has been steady but high). The pain does not wake you at night.
  • No falls recently (apart from the haystack fall in your 30s), no recent fractures, and no breaks from a minor fall.
  • No weakness, numbness or pins and needles in the legs. No problems controlling your bladder or bowels. No numbness around the bottom.
  • No stomach ulcers, reflux, kidney problems, heart problems or high blood pressure that you know of.

Past medical history:

  • You broke both knees in a fall from a haystack on the farm in your 30s. They were in plaster for a few months and you had no operation.
  • You are overweight. If asked, you were told your BMI is 32. "I've tried diets before but I can never stick to them."
  • Your periods stopped at 51. No hormone replacement therapy.
  • Nothing else.

Medications: a multivitamin every day for 5 years. You haven't taken anything for the pain. Allergies: peanuts (rash and lip swelling as a child). No drug allergies. Vaccinations: "I'm honestly not sure what I've had."

Family history: your mother "has pain in her joints and hips too, but I don't remember what from." Your father died of prostate cancer at 59. Your son is healthy. As far as you know nobody in the family has rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis or bowel disease.

Social history:

  • You smoke 2 cigarettes a day and have done for 10 years. You used to smoke marijuana but no longer do.
  • Alcohol: about 4 standard drinks a week.
  • "Unfortunately I've let myself get a bit lazy since my son took over most of the work on the farm 8 years ago. I only manage a short walk a couple of times a week, and I have to stop and rest now."
  • "I eat lots of fatty foods and drink a lot of sweetened drinks."
  • You live with your partner and son in a regional town an hour from the city. You are well connected with friends and the community.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "Not sure, I think I'm just getting old!" You are worried that you will not be able to keep helping on the farm. You would like something to help with the pain so you can keep walking around the farm and manage around the house.

If asked something outside the script, give a realistic answer that fits the story.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: comfortable at rest. Slow, slightly antalgic gait, with stiffness getting up from the chair.
  • Vital signs and measurements: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 76 beats/min regular, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C. Weight 87 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 32, waist 102 cm.
  • Hands, inspection: firm swellings at the DIP joints of both hands (Heberden's nodes) and at several PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes). Squaring of both thumb bases. No redness. No ulnar deviation, swan-neck or boutonnière deformity. No nail pitting or onycholysis, no psoriatic plaques. No rheumatoid nodules at the elbows and no tophi.
  • Hands, palpation: the swellings are hard and bony, not soft or boggy. No warmth. MCP squeeze test negative and the MCPs are not swollen. The thumb bases (first CMC joints) are tender, with crepitus on the grind test.
  • Hands, function: grip and pinch weaker than expected, and slow to open a jar or undo a button. Full fist possible but slightly reduced flexion at the DIP joints.
  • Knees: mild varus alignment on both sides, with mild quadriceps wasting. Bony enlargement at the joint margins. No warmth. No effusion (patellar tap and bulge sign negative). Coarse crepitus through movement on both sides. Flexion to 110° both sides, painful at the end of range. Ligaments stable.
  • Hips: internal rotation reduced on both sides (about 15°) and reproduces groin pain. Flexion slightly reduced. No tenderness over the greater trochanters.
  • Lumbar spine: normal alignment. Mild paraspinal tenderness on both sides, no midline bony tenderness. Flexion and extension reduced and uncomfortable. Straight leg raise negative on both sides. Power, sensation and reflexes in the legs normal.
  • Other: shoulders move fully without pain or tenderness over the shoulder girdle. Temporal arteries non-tender with normal pulses. No rash, no mouth ulcers, eyes normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self by name and role, confirms the patient's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Empathic and non-judgemental, including when discussing her weight, diet and smoking; uses plain language and checks understanding.
History
Characterises the joint pain:

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual over 6 months, worsening; no trigger.
Sites, on both sides: lower back, hips, knees and hands (DIPs, PIPs and thumb bases).
Character and severity: deep ache, 5/10 at worst.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse with movement and weight-bearing, better with rest (mechanical).

check.x: Asks how long morning stiffness lasts (under 30 minutes, gone after her first cup of tea).
Asks about crepitus (clicking) and reduced range of movement.
Asks about the impact on function and work: difficulty with the 15-minute walk around the farm and with opening jars.
Screens for clusters of symptoms of other causes of polyarticular pain:
check.d: Credit each sub-item for at least one relevant question about it; 9.1 (RA) and 9.6 (red flags) need at least two.

kids.x: Rheumatoid arthritis: prolonged morning stiffness (over 30 to 60 minutes), soft or hot joint swelling, rheumatoid nodules, fatigue.
Polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis: shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms.
SLE: rash, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, hair loss, Raynaud's phenomenon.
Gout or pseudogout: a sudden, very painful, hot swollen joint, previous attacks.
Spondyloarthritis: psoriasis or nail changes (psoriatic), diarrhoea or rectal bleeding (enteropathic), recent infection, urethritis or red eyes (reactive).
Red flags: fever, weight loss, night pain, falls or low-trauma fractures, and leg weakness, numbness or bladder or bowel change with the back pain.

check.x: Takes a past history that identifies the risk factors: both knees fractured in her 30s, obesity (BMI 32) with difficulty sustaining lifestyle change, menopause at 51.

Takes a medication and safety history: current medicines and analgesia tried (multivitamin only, none for pain), allergies (peanut, no drug allergy), and asks about peptic ulcer, kidney or heart disease (NSAID safety).
Asks about family history of joint disease, including inflammatory arthritis or psoriasis (mother has joint and hip pain; none known).
Takes a social history covering occupation and activity level, diet, smoking and alcohol.
Explores her ideas ("just getting old"), concerns (keeping up on the farm) and expectations (pain relief to stay active).
Examination
Asks for vital signs and weight, height, BMI and waist (BMI 32), and observes her gait and how she gets up from the chair.
Examines both hands (look, feel, move, function):

kids.x: Inspection: Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, squaring of the thumb bases; looks for and finds no rheumatoid deformities, nail pitting, psoriasis, nodules or tophi.
Palpation: the swellings are hard and bony with no warmth or synovitis, and the MCP squeeze test is negative; thumb base tenderness with crepitus on the grind test.
Function: grip, pinch and fine tasks (jar, button) are reduced.

check.x: Examines both knees: alignment (varus), quadriceps wasting, warmth, effusion (patellar tap or bulge sign), crepitus, range of movement and stability.
Examines both hips: range of movement, finding reduced internal rotation that reproduces groin pain; checks for trochanteric tenderness.
Examines the lumbar spine (midline and paraspinal tenderness, range) and screens the legs neurologically (straight leg raise, power, sensation, reflexes).
Looks for features of other causes (any two of: shoulder girdle tenderness or range, temporal arteries, rash, mouth ulcers, eyes).
Interpretation
Inflammatory markers and serology: normal CRP (4) and ESR (16) and negative RF and anti-CCP, which argue against rheumatoid arthritis, other inflammatory arthritis and PMR.
FBC and UEC: no anaemia or raised white cell count, and normal kidney function (eGFR over 90), so renal function does not rule out an NSAID if one is needed.
Hand X-ray: symmetrical joint space narrowing at the DIP, PIP and first CMC joints, with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis, in keeping with nodal (generalised) osteoarthritis.
Notes what is absent on the X-ray: no erosions, no periarticular osteopenia and no chondrocalcinosis, which argue against rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout and CPPD.
States that osteoarthritis is mainly a clinical diagnosis. The tests were done to exclude inflammatory arthritis, and X-rays of the knees and hips are not needed to make the diagnosis.
Management

Explains the diagnosis in plain words (cartilage wear with the joint's attempt at repair, common, not simply 'old age', and improves with active treatment) and corrects her idea that it is "just getting old".
Recommends exercise as core treatment: a regular, progressive strengthening and aerobic program (for example walking, hydrotherapy), explaining that it reduces pain and improves function.
Recommends weight loss, aiming to lose at least 5% of body weight (ideally around 10%), with a practical plan (e.g. cutting sugary drinks and fatty foods, or dietitian referral).
Arranges multidisciplinary care, naming a GP Chronic Condition Management Plan (GPCCMP; it replaced the GPMP and TCA from July 2025) for Medicare-subsidised allied health (up to 5 visits a year):

kids.x: Physiotherapist: tailored exercise program.
Dietitian: a sustainable weight-loss plan.
Occupational therapist: hand joint protection, aids (e.g. jar opener) and a thumb base splint.

check.x: Gives a stepwise, safe medicine plan:
check.d: Critical fail on item 33 if the candidate starts an oral NSAID without any risk assessment (33.2) or offers an opioid (33.3).

kids.x: A topical NSAID first for the hands and knees.

If an oral NSAID is mentioned, it is offered only if needed, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, after checking GI, kidney and cardiovascular risk and BP, with a PPI if GI risk is high (mark not applicable if no oral NSAID is offered).
Does not offer opioids, explaining to her that opioids are not recommended for osteoarthritis.
States that paracetamol has limited benefit, so it is not first-line.
States glucosamine (and chondroitin) is not recommended.

check.x: Names at least one next step: an intra-articular corticosteroid injection for a painful knee or hip, or orthopaedic referral if severe hip or knee OA persists despite non-surgical care.
Safety netting

Gives specific red flags in plain words: a hot, red, swollen joint or fever (same-day GP or ED); new soft joint swelling or stiffness lasting hours (see the GP soon); back pain with leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the bottom, or bladder or bowel problems (go to ED).
If an oral NSAID is offered, tells her to stop it and seek help for indigestion, black stools or vomiting blood (ED), ankle swelling, breathlessness or passing less urine.
check.d: Applies only if the candidate offers an oral NSAID; otherwise not applicable and not a critical fail.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review in 4 to 6 weeks to review pain, function and weight and to complete the care plan, with blood pressure and kidney function checks if an oral NSAID is started, then regular review.

part2.lead: Ms Thomas had blood tests and X-rays of both hands at the regional hospital this week, and has come back to discuss the results. Here they are.
part2.patient: Ms Thomas does not interject in Part 2; her questions are built into questions 3 and 4. She is keen to stay active on the farm.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected at the regional hospital pathology collection centre this week. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: CRP 4 mg/L and ESR 16 mm/h are within range. RF is under 10 IU/mL and anti-CCP is 1.1 U/mL, both negative. Hb 138, WCC 6.8 and platelets 265 are normal. Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine 60 and eGFR over 90 are normal.

For Ms Thomas: normal inflammatory markers fit osteoarthritis, which has only a low-grade inflammatory component, so markers are normal or only slightly raised. They argue against rheumatoid arthritis, other inflammatory arthritis and PMR (where the ESR and CRP are usually raised). Negative RF and anti-CCP make rheumatoid arthritis much less likely, especially with no synovitis on examination. There is no anaemia of chronic disease.

What it changes: no rheumatology referral is needed. Normal kidney function means an oral NSAID is not ruled out on renal grounds if she needs one, and this is the baseline for monitoring.

handover.label: X-ray of both hands
handover.result:
Examination: X-ray of both hands and wrists, PA and oblique views.

Clinical details: 56-year-old woman with 6 months of gradually worsening pain in both hands, knees, hips and the lower back, worse with use, and morning stiffness under 30 minutes. Firm swellings of the DIP and PIP joints and the thumb bases. ?Osteoarthritis ?inflammatory arthritis.

Comparison: none.

Findings:

  • Alignment: no subluxation, ulnar deviation or collapse deformity.
  • Joint spaces: symmetrical narrowing in both hands, most marked at the DIP joints, also at the PIP joints, the first carpometacarpal (thumb base) joints and the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joints, with mild narrowing of the MCP joints.
  • Bone margins: marginal osteophytes at the DIP and PIP joints, corresponding to the clinical Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, and at both first carpometacarpal joints. No hook-like osteophytes at the MCP heads.
  • Subchondral bone: subchondral sclerosis at the DIP and first carpometacarpal joints. No subchondral cysts seen.
  • Erosions and bone density: no marginal or central erosions. No periarticular osteopenia; bone density looks normal for age.
  • Soft tissues: bony swelling around the DIP and PIP joints. No soft tissue calcification and no chondrocalcinosis at the triangular fibrocartilage.
  • Other: no fracture.

Conclusion: symmetrical polyarticular degenerative change in both hands (DIP, PIP, first carpometacarpal and scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joints, with mild MCP involvement), with joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis, in keeping with osteoarthritis. No erosions or other features of inflammatory or crystal arthritis.
handover.model:
Read (LOSS): symmetrical loss of joint space, worst at the DIP joints and also at the PIP joints, the thumb bases and the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joints. Osteophytes match the Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, and there is subchondral sclerosis. No subchondral cysts are seen. There are no erosions, no periarticular osteopenia, no chondrocalcinosis and no fracture.

For Ms Thomas: the distribution (DIPs, PIPs, thumb base) and the features are typical of nodal hand osteoarthritis. This fits her examination and her knee, hip and spine symptoms as generalised osteoarthritis. The absent erosions and osteopenia argue against rheumatoid arthritis. There is no pencil-in-cup change of psoriatic arthritis and no punched-out erosions of gout. The mild MCP narrowing has no hook osteophytes or chondrocalcinosis, so haemochromatosis or CPPD arthropathy is not suggested.

What it changes: it confirms the clinical diagnosis. Knee and hip X-rays are not needed to diagnose osteoarthritis and would not change her first-line management.

ask: You are now presenting Ms Thomas to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Ms Thomas, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer, including why each of these tests was requested.
Outline your management of Ms Thomas now, here in general practice, including how you would answer her request for 'something strong' for the pain and her question about glucosamine.
Before Ms Thomas goes home, what would you tell her, including whether this is 'just getting old' and whether she will need new knees, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year student at the practice. Laila Thomas, 56, farmer.
  • Situation: 6 months of gradually worsening pain on both sides in the hands, knees, hips and lower back, limiting her farm walk and opening jars.
  • Background: mechanical pain, stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus. Both knees fractured in her 30s. BMI 32. Mother has joint pain. Smokes 2 a day. Multivitamin only. Peanut allergy.
  • Assessment: Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, squared thumb bases, knee crepitus, reduced hip internal rotation, no synovitis. CRP and ESR normal, RF and anti-CCP negative: no inflammatory arthritis. FBC normal, eGFR over 90. Hand X-ray: DIP, PIP and CMC narrowing with osteophytes and sclerosis, no erosions. Generalised osteoarthritis.
  • Recommendation: Please review; plan exercise, weight loss, allied health via GPCCMP, topical NSAID, review 4 to 6 weeks. (Optional: smoking cessation via Quitline.)

Most likely: generalised (nodal) osteoarthritis of the hands, knees, hips and lumbar spine. For it: age, gradual mechanical pain, stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus, bony nodes, previous knee fractures, BMI 32, mother affected, and an X-ray showing narrowing, osteophytes and sclerosis.

Tests: CRP and ESR to exclude inflammation, RF and anti-CCP for RA, X-ray to confirm the hand pattern and look for erosions. FBC for anaemia of chronic disease and a raised white cell count; UEC as a renal baseline before any oral NSAID. Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetrical small joints. Against it: short stiffness, bony swelling, DIPs affected, normal markers, negative serology, no erosions.
  • PMR: over 50 with hip pain. Against it: no girdle stiffness, normal ESR and CRP.
  • Psoriatic arthritis: DIPs. Against it: no psoriasis or nail change, no erosions.
  • Gout or CPPD: no acute attacks, tophi or chondrocalcinosis.
  • Vertebral fracture or malignancy: no red flags.

1. Explain and educate: common and treatable, not "just old age"; self-management with written information.
  2. Exercise (core): progressive strengthening and aerobic program, hydrotherapy.
  3. Weight loss: at least 5% of body weight, ideally about 10%.
  4. GPCCMP: physio, dietitian, OT.
  5. Medicines: topical NSAID first; oral NSAID only with a risk check and a PPI if needed; paracetamol of limited benefit; no opioids; glucosamine not recommended. If still limited: corticosteroid injection or orthopaedic referral.

• In plain words: wear of the joint cartilage. Staying active and losing weight are the most effective treatments. Exercise will not damage her joints.
  • Red flags: a hot, red, swollen joint or fever: same-day GP or ED. New soft swelling or stiffness lasting hours: see the GP. Back pain with leg weakness or numbness, numbness around the bottom, or bladder or bowel problems: ED.
  • NSAID warnings (if an oral NSAID is offered): stop and seek help for indigestion, black stools or vomiting blood (ED), ankle swelling, breathlessness or passing less urine.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 4 to 6 weeks for pain, function and weight, and to complete the care plan. Check BP and kidney function if an oral NSAID is started. Then regular review.

ddx.dx: Generalised (nodal) osteoarthritis of the hands, knees, hips and lumbar spine
ddx.for: Gradual mechanical pain worse on weight-bearing, stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus, Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, previous knee fractures, BMI 32, an affected mother, and X-ray narrowing with osteophytes and sclerosis.
ddx.against: Mild MCP narrowing on X-ray is less typical of primary osteoarthritis.

ddx.for: Symmetrical polyarticular small-joint hand involvement with MCP narrowing on X-ray.
ddx.against: Stiffness under 30 minutes, hard bony swelling without synovitis, DIPs involved, normal CRP and ESR, negative RF and anti-CCP, and no erosions.

ddx.for: Over 50 with hip and lower back pain and morning stiffness.
ddx.against: No shoulder or hip girdle stiffness, stiffness settles within 30 minutes, small hand joints affected, and ESR and CRP are normal.

ddx.for: DIP joint involvement and lower back pain.
ddx.against: No psoriasis, nail pitting, bowel symptoms, recent infection or eye inflammation, and no erosions or pencil-in-cup change.

ddx.dx: Gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
ddx.for: Middle-aged with obesity and a diet high in sugary drinks; DIP/PIP swellings could be mistaken for tophi.
ddx.against: No episodes of sudden hot swollen joints, no tophi and no chondrocalcinosis on X-ray.

ddx.dx: Osteoporotic vertebral fracture or spinal malignancy causing back pain
ddx.for: Postmenopausal woman of 56 who smokes, with lower back pain.
ddx.against: Gradual mechanical pain on both sides with no night pain, weight loss, fever, falls, midline tenderness or neurological signs.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. A candidate who screens for differentials while taking the history earns item 9. Credit each sub-item for at least one relevant question about it; 9.1 (RA) and 9.6 (red flags) need at least two. In Part 2 hand over both results together and ask all four questions in order. Ms Thomas's questions are built into questions 3 and 4; she does not interject. Credit item 27 whenever the candidate says osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis, whether in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. Credit item 29 in either the management or the final question. For item 32, accept GPMP/TCA as equivalent. Item 33.2 and item 37 apply only if the candidate offers an oral NSAID; otherwise mark them not applicable and do not count item 37 as a critical fail. Critical fail on item 33 if the candidate starts an oral NSAID without any risk assessment (33.2) or offers an opioid (33.3). Credit item 34 if given in answer to "Will I end up needing new knees?" or in any Part 2 answer.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain and pins down the short morning stiffness, the crepitus and the impact on function. They screen for RA, PMR and GCA, SLE, crystal arthritis, spondyloarthritis and red flags, and identify the risk factors (knee fractures, obesity, family history). On examination they separate bony nodes from synovitis. In Part 2 they read normal markers and negative serology as against inflammatory arthritis, and read the hand X-ray systematically. They put exercise and weight loss first, with a multidisciplinary team through a GP Chronic Condition Management Plan, and give a stepwise, safe plan for medicines. They finish with specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a pain history without asking how long the stiffness lasts or screening for other causes. They examine only one joint, or miss that the hand swellings are bony. They may lead with paracetamol or opioids, order knee and hip MRI or arthroscopy, agree that it is "just old age", or end with "come back if it gets worse".
explain:
Diagnosis: generalised osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis is a disease of the whole joint. The articular cartilage breaks down mechanically, and the bone tries to repair it, forming osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis. There is also a low-grade inflammatory component. That is why patients have brief stiffness after rest and why inflammatory markers are normal or only slightly raised. Ms Thomas has the typical features: age over 45, gradual pain worse with weight-bearing and better with rest, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus, reduced range, and hard bony enlargement of the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes) and thumb bases. Her knees, hips and lumbar spine are also involved.

Risk factors: age, female sex, obesity, previous joint injury (her knee fractures), physically demanding work (farming is linked with hip osteoarthritis), and family history (her mother). Secondary causes are abnormal joint forces, trauma, previous inflammatory arthritis and haemochromatosis. Common sites are the DIP joints, the first CMC joint (taps and jars), knees, hips and spine.

Telling osteoarthritis from inflammatory arthritis

  • Rheumatoid arthritis: morning stiffness over 30 to 60 minutes, soft boggy swelling of the MCPs, PIPs and wrists (DIPs usually spared), nodules, fatigue, raised CRP and ESR, positive RF or anti-CCP, and periarticular osteopenia and erosions on X-ray.
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica: over 50, with shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness and a raised ESR and CRP. Ask about GCA symptoms (headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual change), because GCA threatens vision.
  • SLE: rash, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, Raynaud's, hair loss.
  • Gout and CPPD: acute attacks of a hot swollen joint, tophi, chondrocalcinosis.
  • Spondyloarthritis: psoriasis and nail changes, inflammatory bowel symptoms, a recent infection or urethritis, uveitis, and inflammatory back pain.
  • Red flags: fever, weight loss, night pain and fractures point to infection, malignancy or osteoporosis. Neurological symptoms with back pain need urgent assessment.

Interpreting the results

Osteoarthritis is mainly a clinical diagnosis. The RACGP knee and hip guideline and the ACSQHC Osteoarthritis of the Knee Clinical Care Standard advise that imaging is not needed to diagnose a typical presentation. Here the tests were done to exclude inflammatory arthritis, because her small hand joints are involved in a symmetrical pattern. CRP and ESR are normal, and RF and anti-CCP are negative. The hand X-ray shows the LOSS features: Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis and Subchondral cysts (cysts are absent here). There are no erosions or periarticular osteopenia. MCP involvement is less typical of primary osteoarthritis. Prominent 2nd and 3rd MCP disease with hook osteophytes or chondrocalcinosis should prompt iron studies for haemochromatosis and consideration of CPPD. Neither feature is present here. Normal kidney function is the baseline if an oral NSAID is needed.

Management (eTG, RACGP)

  • Education and self-management: explain that osteoarthritis is common, is not simply ageing, and that activity helps rather than harms the joints.
  • Exercise: land-based strengthening and aerobic exercise is the core treatment for knee and hip osteoarthritis. It reduces pain and improves function. Hydrotherapy and tai chi are alternatives. A physiotherapist can tailor the program and provide a walking aid if needed.
  • Weight loss: strongly recommended for anyone overweight with knee or hip osteoarthritis. Losing at least 5% of body weight (ideally around 10%) improves pain and function. A dietitian helps her make it sustainable.
  • Hand osteoarthritis: joint protection with an occupational therapist. That means avoiding prolonged grip and repetitive thumb strain, and using large-grip tools, jar openers and other gadgets, pacing, and a thumb base splint.
  • Medicines: topical NSAIDs are suited to superficial joints such as the hands and knees; topical capsaicin is an option for knee OA. Oral NSAIDs can be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, after assessing GI, kidney and cardiovascular risk and blood pressure, with a PPI if GI risk is raised. Paracetamol has limited benefit. Opioids are not recommended. Glucosamine and chondroitin are not recommended (RACGP recommends against them); most supplements have no proven benefit.
  • Procedures: an intra-articular corticosteroid injection (image-guided for the hip) for short-term relief of a painful knee or hip. Arthroscopic lavage or debridement is not recommended. Refer for joint replacement when severe hip or knee osteoarthritis keeps causing pain and loss of function despite good non-surgical care.
  • Coordinating care: a GP Chronic Condition Management Plan gives her up to 5 Medicare-subsidised allied health visits a year (physiotherapist, dietitian, occupational therapist). It replaced the GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangements from 1 July 2025. This matters for someone living an hour from the city.
  • General health: stopping smoking (Quitline) and keeping alcohol within the NHMRC guidelines. Check her vaccinations on the Australian Immunisation Register (AIR): tetanus booster as a farmer, Q fever screening and vaccination if she works with livestock, annual influenza, and discuss zoster vaccine.

Safety netting

Tell her to seek same-day care for a hot, red, swollen joint or fever (possible septic or crystal arthritis). She should return for new soft swelling or long morning stiffness (possible inflammatory arthritis). Back pain with leg weakness or numbness, saddle numbness, or bladder or bowel change means going to ED. If she starts an oral NSAID, tell her the warning signs of GI bleeding, kidney injury and fluid retention. Review her in 4 to 6 weeks to check progress against agreed goals (her farm walk, opening jars) and her weight.
points: Gradual mechanical pain in the DIPs, PIPs, thumb bases, knees, hips and spine, with morning stiffness under 30 minutes and hard bony nodes, is osteoarthritis. Stiffness lasting over 30 to 60 minutes or soft synovial swelling suggests inflammatory arthritis.

Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis. Inflammatory markers are normal or only slightly raised, and tests (CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP, X-ray) are used to exclude inflammatory arthritis, not to diagnose osteoarthritis.
On X-ray, osteoarthritis shows LOSS: loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts. It has no erosions or periarticular osteopenia.

Exercise and weight loss (if overweight, aim to lose at least 5% of body weight, ideally around 10%) are the core treatments. Coordinate physiotherapy, dietetics and occupational therapy through a GP Chronic Condition Management Plan (GPCCMP), which replaced the GPMP and TCA from July 2025 and gives up to 5 Medicare-subsidised allied health visits a year.

Use topical NSAIDs first and oral NSAIDs at the lowest dose for the shortest time after checking GI, kidney and cardiovascular risk. Paracetamol has limited benefit, opioids and arthroscopy are not recommended, and joint replacement is for severe hip or knee osteoarthritis despite non-surgical care.
